title: Correspondence (Set-Valued Map)
content: Defines a correspondence $F: S \to 2^S$ as a structure bundling four properties: the underlying function `toFun`, nonemptiness of values, closedness of values, and the maps-to constraint $F(x) \subseteq S$. This is the standard formulation from mathematical economics (Berge 1959), where correspondences model budget sets, best-response maps, and supply/demand relations.
mathContext: A correspondence from $S$ to itself is a function $F: S \to 2^S$ such that for all $x \in S$: (1) $F(x) \neq \emptyset$, (2) $F(x)$ is closed, (3) $F(x) \subseteq S$.

title: Set-Valued Fixed Points
content: Defines fixed points for correspondences: $x^*$ is a fixed point of $F$ if $x^* \in F(x^*)$. This generalizes the classical fixed point equation $f(x^*) = x^*$ — instead of equality, we require membership. The `HasFixedPoint` predicate asserts existence of such a point.
mathContext: For a correspondence $F: S \to 2^S$, a fixed point is $x^* \in S$ with $x^* \in F(x^*)$. For singleton-valued $F(x) = \{f(x)\}$, this reduces to $f(x^*) = x^*$.

title: Convex-Valued Correspondences
content: Defines the convexity condition on correspondence values: for every $x \in S$, the image $F(x)$ must be convex over $\mathbb{R}$. This is a critical hypothesis of Kakutani's theorem — without convexity, the theorem fails. The classic counterexample is the rotation map on $S^1$ viewed as a set-valued map with non-convex images.
mathContext: $F$ is convex-valued if for all $x \in S$, $F(x)$ is convex: $\forall y,z \in F(x),\, \forall \lambda \in [0,1],\, \lambda y + (1-\lambda)z \in F(x)$.

title: Upper Hemicontinuity (Berge 1959)
content: Defines upper hemicontinuity using Berge's neighborhood formulation: $F$ is UHC at $x$ if for every open set $V \supseteq F(x)$, there is a neighborhood $U$ of $x$ such that $F(y) \subseteq V$ for all $y \in U \cap S$. This is strictly weaker than lower hemicontinuity and equivalent to the closed-graph property when $F$ has compact values.
mathContext: $F: S \to 2^S$ is upper hemicontinuous if $\forall x \in S,\, \forall V \text{ open with } F(x) \subseteq V,\, \exists U \in \mathcal{N}(x),\, \forall y \in U \cap S,\, F(y) \subseteq V$.

title: Continuous Functions Induce UHC Correspondences
content: Proves that any continuous function $f: \alpha \to \alpha$ induces an upper hemicontinuous singleton correspondence $x \mapsto \{f(x)\}$. The proof reduces UHC to the preimage characterization of continuity: if $V$ is open and $f(x) \in V$, then $f^{-1}(V)$ is an open neighborhood of $x$, and any $y$ in this preimage satisfies $\{f(y)\} \subseteq V$.
mathContext: If $f$ is continuous and $F(x) = \{f(x)\}$, then $F$ is UHC. Proof: given open $V \supseteq \{f(x)\}$, take $U = f^{-1}(V)$, which is open by continuity.

title: Brouwer FPT for Compact Convex Sets (Proved)
content: States and **proves** the Brouwer Fixed Point Theorem for the closed unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^n$: every continuous self-map of $\text{ClosedBall}(n)$ has a fixed point (`brouwer_compact_convex`). This was *previously axiomatized*; it is now derived from the parent Brouwer FPT in `BrouwerFixedPoint.lean` (proved there via the no-retraction theorem) by wrapping the map in a `Brouwer.SelfMap` and applying that result. The section first sets up `ClosedBall n` together with the supporting lemmas `closedBall_compact`, `closedBall_nonempty`, and `closedBall_convex`, which supply the compact-convex hypotheses the fixed-point theorem needs.
mathContext: If $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is nonempty, compact, and convex and $f: S \to S$ is continuous, then $\exists x^* \in S,\ f(x^*) = x^*$. Here $S = \text{ClosedBall}(n)$ and the result is obtained from the parent no-retraction proof, not assumed.

title: Kakutani FPT — Axiom with Classical Proof Sketch
content: Axiomatizes the Kakutani Fixed Point Theorem with a detailed proof sketch. The classical proof (Kakutani 1941) works by triangulating $S$ into simplices of mesh $1/k$, selecting points $y_i \in F(v_i)$ at vertices, extending affinely to get $f_k: S \to S$, applying Brouwer to get fixed points $x_k$, and taking a convergent subsequence. Upper hemicontinuity ensures the limit $x^*$ satisfies $x^* \in F(x^*)$. This is axiomatized because the triangulation/approximation argument requires tools beyond current Mathlib.
mathContext: **Kakutani (1941)**: Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty, compact, convex. If $F: S \to 2^S$ is UHC with nonempty convex closed values, then $\exists x^* \in S$ with $x^* \in F(x^*)$.

title: Singleton Correspondence Construction
content: Constructs the singleton correspondence $F(x) = \{f(x)\}$ from a continuous self-map $f$, verifying all four correspondence properties: singletons are nonempty, singletons are closed, and if $f$ maps $S$ to $S$ then $\{f(x)\} \subseteq S$. Also proves singleton convexity (singletons are trivially convex). This is the technical bridge that shows Kakutani strictly generalizes Brouwer.
mathContext: Given continuous $f: S \to S$, define $F(x) = \{f(x)\}$. Then $F$ is a correspondence with convex values, and $F$ is UHC (by the previous theorem).

title: Kakutani Implies Brouwer (Constructive Proof)
content: Two key results: (1) `kakutani_singleton_iff_brouwer` shows that a fixed point of $\{f(x)\}$ at $x^*$ is equivalent to $f(x^*) = x^*$ — proved by simplification and `tauto`. (2) `brouwer_from_kakutani` derives the full Brouwer theorem from Kakutani: construct the singleton correspondence, verify UHC and convexity, apply Kakutani, then extract the classical fixed point from set membership. This constructively demonstrates that Kakutani is a proper generalization.
mathContext: $x^* \in \{f(x^*)\} \iff f(x^*) = x^*$. Therefore Brouwer's theorem is a corollary of Kakutani's: apply Kakutani to $F(x) = \{f(x)\}$.

title: Continuous Interval Correspondence
content: Defines a 1D interval correspondence $F(x) = [l(x), u(x)]$ on $[0,1]$ where both bound functions are continuous. The structure bundles seven properties: $l(x) \leq u(x)$, $0 \leq l(x)$, $u(x) \leq 1$, and continuity of both bounds on $[0,1]$. Fixed points satisfy $l(x) \leq x \leq u(x)$, meaning $x \in F(x) = [l(x), u(x)]$.
mathContext: An interval correspondence on $[0,1]$ is $F(x) = [l(x), u(x)]$ where $l, u: [0,1] \to [0,1]$ are continuous with $l(x) \leq u(x)$. A fixed point satisfies $l(x^*) \leq x^* \leq u(x^*)$.

title: 1D Kakutani via Intermediate Value Theorem (Fully Proved)
content: Proves the 1D Kakutani theorem without any axioms using the IVT. The key idea: define $g(x) = u(x) - x$. Since $g(0) = u(0) \geq l(0) \geq 0$ and $g(1) = u(1) - 1 \leq 0$, the IVT gives $x_0 \in [0,1]$ with $g(x_0) = 0$, i.e., $u(x_0) = x_0$. Then $l(x_0) \leq u(x_0) = x_0 \leq u(x_0)$, so $x_0$ is a fixed point. This is the only fully proved case of Kakutani in this formalization.
mathContext: Define $g(x) = u(x) - x$. Then $g(0) \geq 0$ and $g(1) \leq 0$. By the IVT, $\exists x_0 \in [0,1]$ with $u(x_0) = x_0$. Since $l(x_0) \leq u(x_0) = x_0$, we get $x_0 \in F(x_0)$.

title: Correspondence Algebra: Constant and Identity
content: Builds basic correspondence algebra: (1) the constant correspondence $F(x) = S$ trivially has every point as a fixed point; (2) the identity correspondence $F(x) = \{x\}$ makes every point a fixed point. These are the simplest instances verifying the correspondence framework. The constant correspondence proof uses compactness of the closed ball to show closedness of values.
mathContext: The constant correspondence $F(x) = S$ has $\forall x \in S,\, x \in S = F(x)$. The identity $F(x) = \{x\}$ has $x \in \{x\} = F(x)$ for all $x \in S$.

title: Mixed Strategy Spaces: Compact, Convex, Closed
content: Proves the three fundamental properties of mixed strategy simplices $\Delta_k = \{\sigma \in \mathbb{R}^k \mid \sigma_i \geq 0,\, \sum \sigma_i = 1\}$: (1) convexity — convex combinations of probability distributions are distributions; (2) closedness — intersection of halfspaces $\{\sigma_i \geq 0\}$ and the hyperplane $\{\sum \sigma_i = 1\}$; (3) compactness — as a closed subset of the bounded box $[0,1]^k$. These are the prerequisites for applying Kakutani to game theory.
mathContext: The simplex $\Delta_k = \{\sigma \in \mathbb{R}^k : \sigma_i \geq 0,\, \sum_i \sigma_i = 1\}$ is compact (closed and bounded in $\mathbb{R}^k$) and convex.

title: Nash Equilibrium Framework
content: Defines an $N$-player finite game and proves that the product of mixed strategy simplices is compact — the first step toward Nash's existence proof. Nash (1950) applied Kakutani to the best-response correspondence on this product space: each player's best response to others' strategies forms a nonempty convex compact set, and the combined correspondence is UHC. The fixed point is a Nash equilibrium where no player can unilaterally improve.
mathContext: A finite $N$-player game has strategy counts $(k_1, \ldots, k_N)$. The mixed strategy space $\prod_{i=1}^N \Delta_{k_i}$ is compact (product of compact sets). Nash's theorem: $\exists \sigma^* \in \prod \Delta_{k_i}$ such that $\sigma^*_i$ is a best response to $\sigma^*_{-i}$ for all $i$.

title: UHC Closure Properties
content: Proves two closure properties of upper hemicontinuity: (1) constant correspondences $F(x) = C$ are trivially UHC — the neighborhood is all of $\alpha$; (2) continuous images preserve UHC — if $F$ is UHC and $g$ is continuous, then $x \mapsto g(F(x))$ is UHC. The second result uses the fact that $g^{-1}(V)$ is open when $V$ is open and $g$ is continuous, then applies UHC of $F$ to the preimage.
mathContext: If $F$ is UHC and $g$ is continuous, then $G(x) = g(F(x))$ is UHC. Proof: given open $V \supseteq G(x)$, note $F(x) \subseteq g^{-1}(V)$ which is open, so UHC of $F$ gives the required neighborhood.
